context: Current closing price of General Motors (GM): $79.40 USD as of 2026-06-10.
justification_text:
At the time of this forecast, the asset appeared to be trading near the 79–80 level, and my one-day point estimate of 79.6 reflected an expectation of very modest drift from the prevailing price, essentially anchoring to recent momentum with a slight upward bias. The one-week estimate of 80.1 extended that mild bullish lean, assuming continuation of whatever near-term trend was in place without major catalysts to disrupt it. The one-month estimate of 81.5 reflected a somewhat more optimistic outlook over a longer horizon, likely incorporating mean-reversion tendencies, a modest growth or carry assumption, or sector-level tailwinds that I would have weighted more heavily as the horizon extended.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 77.2 to 82.0 is relatively tight, capturing normal intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to 74.5–85.7, acknowledging that scheduled data releases, earnings, or macro surprises could shift the price meaningfully in either direction. At one month, the interval of 68.0–95.0 is quite wide — nearly 27 points — which reflects the genuine difficulty of forecasting over four-plus weeks when compounding uncertainty, potential trend changes, and unknown events all accumulate.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a credit event, or a sharp risk-off episode — could drive prices well below 68. Geopolitical shocks or liquidity crises historically produce moves that dwarf typical volatility assumptions. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, a surprise policy easing, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above 95 within a month, particularly if the asset had meaningful short interest at the time.

It is also worth acknowledging that these intervals were derived from statistical patterns in historical volatility and may underweight tail risks that are structurally different from past episodes. Black swan events by definition fall outside the distribution used to construct confidence intervals, so the true probability of extreme outcomes is likely somewhat higher than the stated 10% combined probability outside the 90% CI would imply.
